title: Wills - LEUKOCORIA: THE WHITE PUPILLARY REFLEX
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Leukocoria, detailing the life-threatening and sight-threatening conditions associated with a white pupillary reflex. This poster covers differential diagnosis, exhaustive workup protocols, and multi-modal treatment strategies from Retinoblastoma to PFV.

sections.title: Definition & Visual Presentation
sections.content: Definition: A white pupillary reflex (see Figure 8.1.1). Figure 8.1.1 Leukocoria.

sections.title: Primary Etiology: Retinoblastoma
content: A malignant tumor of the retina.
Presentation: White, nodular mass.
Endophytic: Breaks through internal limiting membrane into vitreous.
Exophytic: Subretinal mass lesion often underlying a serous retinal detachment.
Diffuse infiltrating: Diffusely spreading lesion simulating uveitis.
Associated Findings: Iris neovascularization (common with large tumors), Aqueous and vitreous seeding.
Eye Characteristics: Cataract is uncommon; eye is normal in size.
Distribution: May be bilateral, unilateral, or multifocal.
Epidemiology: Diagnosis usually made in patients under years of age (mean age: 18 months).
Genetics: Family history elicited in about 10% of cases.

sections.title: Infectious Etiology: Toxocariasis
content: Nematode infection.
Appearance: Localized, white, elevated granuloma in retina OR diffuse endophthalmitis.
Complications: Localized inflammation, vitreous traction bands, macular dragging, traction retinal detachment, and cataract.
Demographics: Rarely bilateral; usually diagnosed between 6 months and 10 years (may present in adults).
Clinical Clues: History of contact with puppies or eating dirt.
Transmission: Can be acquired prenatally/congenital infection.
Diagnostics: Paracentesis may reveal eosinophils; serum ELISA for Toxocara is positive.

rows: Retinal vascular abnormality (micro/macroaneurysms) usually inferotemporal periphery.
Failure of regression of fetal hyaloid complex; fibrovascular stalk from optic nerve to lens.
Xanthocoria; yellow-colored lipid-rich subretinal fluid/exudate; bullous retinal detachment.
Membrane behind lens placing inward traction on elongated ciliary processes.
Usually associated with a small eye; usually unilateral.
Usually boys in first decade; severe cases in early childhood.
Cataract noted at birth or early in life; no family history/risk factors.
Shallowing of anterior chamber, secondary glaucoma, traction retinal detachment.

sections.title: Other Significant Etiologies
content: Pediatric cataract: Opacity present at birth or first months; unilateral/bilateral; family history or systemic disorder common.
Retinal astrocytoma: Sessile to slightly elevated yellow-white mass; may be calcified; associated with tuberous sclerosis complex or neurofibromatosis; giant drusen on optic nerve.
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP): Predominantly premature children; leukocoria usually from retinal detachment.

sections.title: Comprehensive Differential List
sections.content: Others: Retinal detachment, retinochoroidal coloboma, high myopia or anisometropia, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR), myelinated nerve fibers, uveitis, toxoplasmosis, trauma, cytomegalovirus retinitis, endophthalmitis, retinal dysplasia, incontinentia pigmenti, Norrie disease, and medulloepithelioma.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: History & Exam
content: Step 1: History - Check Age at onset, Family history, Prematurity, contact with puppies, or eating dirt.
Step 2: Ocular Exam - Measure corneal diameters (small eye?), Iris check (neovascularization), Lens inspection (cataract).
Step 3: Essential Screens - Dilated fundus examination and anterior vitreous examination.
Step 4: Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) - Needed for young/uncooperative children, especially if retinoblastoma is suspected.
Step 5: Early Screening - If heritable retinoblastoma is a concern, perform office exam within 1 to 2 weeks of birth.

rows: Used when no view of fundus; looks for calcification (tumor), persistent stalk (optic disc to lens), or RD.
Useful for evaluating Coats disease, ROP, and retinoblastoma.
For bilateral/familial retinoblastoma or advanced Coats. MRI preferred for RB to reduce radiation.
Positive at 1:8 in the vast majority of infected patients.
By pediatrician; specifically for retinal astrocytic hamartoma, RB, or systemic cataracts.

sections.title: CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATION
content: NOTE: Anterior chamber paracentesis in a patient with a retinoblastoma should be avoided as it could lead to tumor cell dissemination.

branches: Retinoblastoma: Chemoreduction, Intra-arterial/Intravitreal/Intracameral chemotherapy, Cryotherapy, Thermotherapy, Laser, Plaque radiotherapy, Enucleation (advanced/refractory), Systemic chemo (metastatic).
Toxocariasis: Topical/Periocular/Systemic Steroids, Vitrectomy (traction/non-improvement), Laser photocoagulation of nematode, Albendazole (only for systemic disease).

sections.title: Treatment: Vascular & Developmental
content: Coats Disease: FA-guided laser to leaking vessels/aneurysms; consider Intravitreal anti-VEGF; External drainage for severe RD; Enucleation for neovascular glaucoma.
PFV: Cataract removal, Retrolental stalk resection, Posterior vitrectomy. Amblyopia treatment (Outcome often poor due to foveal/optic nerve hypoplasia, anisometropia, and deprivation).
Retinal Astrocytoma: Observation.
Pediatric Cataract & ROP: See specific sections (8.12 and 8.2).

content.explanation: Timing depends on diagnosis. If heritable disorders are suspected, refer to Ophthalmic Genetics and screen family members. For RB, frequency depends on tumor type, severity, and germline mutations. External irradiation for RB is rarely used due to secondary tumor risk.
